lines.text: אחר 38 אטר
2. Concr. those who come after, de-
scendants, posterity, Ps. 109, 13. Am. 4,
אַחֲרִית Chald. f. i. q. Heb. אַחֲרִית no.
אָחֳרָן Chald. adj. another, alius, Dan.
אֲחֹרַנִּית adv. (r. אָחַר) backwards,
Gen. 9, 23. 1 Sam. 4, 18. Comp. אָחוֹר.
אֲחַשְׁדַּרְפְּנִים m. plur. Esth. 3, 12. 8, 9.
9, 3. Ezra 8, 36, satraps, the governors
or viceroys of the large provinces among
the ancient Persians, possessing both
civil and military power, and being in
the provinces the representatives of the
sovereign, whose state and splendour
they also rivalled. Single parts or sub-
divisions of these provinces were under
procurators or prefects, פַּחוֹת; the sa-
traps governed only whole provinces.
See Brisson de regio Pers. principatu I.
§ 168. Heeren Ideen T. I. p. 489 sq. ed.
4.—The genuine form of this name,
which has lately been found in the
inscriptions of ancient India, is kśatrapa
i. e. warrior of the host; see Benfey in
Gött. Gel. Anz. 1839. p. 805 sq. Lassen
Zeitschr. f. d. Morgenl. III. p. 161. To
this harsher form corresponds the Greek
ἐξατράπης, ἐξαιθράπης, (Boeckh Corp.
Inscr. no. 2691. c,) whence arose by
degrees the softer σατράπης. The ־ָן is
appended. Comp. אֲחַשְׁתְּרָנִים.
אֲחַשְׁדַּרְפְּנִין Chald. m. plur. i. q. Heb.
אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ Ahasuerus, the Hebrew
form of the name Xerxes, as it would
seem. It is found Esth. 1, 1, and often
in this book; also Ezra 4, 6, where the
order of time would require it to be un-
derstood of Cambyses; and further in
Dan. 9, 1, where it stands for Astyages,
the father of Darius the Mede. The true
native orthography of the name Xerxes
has recently been brought to light from
the cuneiform inscriptions; where it is
written kh-sh-y-â-r-sh-â, which seems
to correspond to the modern Persian
شيرشاه i. e. lion-king; since it is cer-
tain that for the softer pronunciation of
s and sh, as uttered by the modern Per-
sians, the ancient Persians had far harsh-
er sounds, as in the words khshayathiya
i. q. Shah king, khshatrap i. q. Satrap.
From this ancient harsher form, the
Hebrews, by prefixing their prosthetic
Aleph, made אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ Ahashverosh, and
the Greeks Ξέρξης. See St. Martin in
Journal Asiatique III. p. 85. Champol-
lion Précis du Système hiéroglyphique,
Tableau général, Tab. 7. 2. p. 24. Las-
sen üb. d. Keilschrift p. 165; also in Zeit-
schr. f. Kunde des Morgenl. VI. p. 124 sq.
אֲחַשְׁרֹשׁ Esth. 10, 1 in Chethib, for
אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ.
אֲחַשְׁתָּרִי (prob. mule-driver, a name
of Persian origin, see next art.) pr. n. m.
Ahashtari, 1 Chr. 4, 6.
אֲחַשְׁתְּרָנִים plur. m. mules, Pers. استار
estâr, استر ester, a mule, Sanscr. açwa-
tara. Esth. 8, 10, where it is rendered
definite by the addition sons of mares.—
The ־ָן is appended, as in אֲחַשְׁדַּרְפְּנִים.
אַחַת see אֶחָד.
אַט subst. m. (r. אָטַט) 1. a gentle
sound, murmur, whisper, and plur. אִטִּים
concr. mutterers, whisperers, i. e. νεκρο-
μάντεις, necromancers, ventriloquists, im-
itating artificially the supposed murmur
or thin voice of the shades or manes, Is.
19, 3. See under אוֹב.
2. a going softly, gentle motion;
whence often adverbially, אַט, לְאַט, לָאַט,
softly, gently, slowly, e. g. of the still slow
gait of a mourner, 1 K. 21, 27; of water
gently flowing, Is. 8, 6. So לְאִטִּי pr. in
my slow gait, slowly, at my convenience,
Gen. 33, 14.—Also of the manner of act-
ing and speaking; 2 Sam. 18, 5 לְאַט לִי
לַנַּעַר (deal) gently with the young man
for my sake! Job 15, 11 וְדָבָר לָאַט עִמָּךְ
and words gently (spoken) towards thee.
* אָטַד a root not in use; Arab. to be
fast, firm; Conj. II, to make fast, to
confirm.—Hence
אָטָד m. the southern buckthorn, Christ’s
thorn, Rhamnus paliurus Linn. so called
from the firmness of its roots, Judg. 9, 14.
15. Ps. 58, 10. Arab. أَطَلٌ, i. q. the more
usual عَوْسَجٌ.
אֵטוּן m. (by Syriasm for אֲטוּן, r. אָטַן)
thread, yarn, of linen or cotton; in Chald.

line_status.note: The left header word ends in resh, not dalet (no right-angle shoulder/foot), and the middle letter is a het with its gap at the top, not a tav: אַחַר. The right header word is unpointed and its final letter is a resh (rounded top, straight descender), not a lamed — no ascender above the line: אטר. Reading B matches the print.
The printed line shows a short horizontal stroke (maqaf-style affix dash) preceding the qamats and final nun, marking ־ָן as a suffix; Reading B omits this dash.
Under the tav the print shows a T-shaped qamets (bar with stem), not two stacked sheva dots; sheva is under the shin only. Reading A matches; B misreads qamets as sheva.

The print shows a horizontal placeholder stroke (maqaf-like dash) carrying the qamets before the final nun, i.e. "־ָן", not a bare qamets on the nun; the Hebrew word's points otherwise match both readings.

The decisive difference is the vowel under the aleph of the second Hebrew word: the print shows a compound shewa (two vertical dots plus a short bar = hataf patah, אֲ), not a plain qamets as in Reading A. First word has tsere (two horizontal dots), root has qamets + patah; both readings agree there.
